html:
Around 1470 BCE the Egyptian ruler Hatshepsut sent a fleet down the Red Sea to the Land of Punt, a country of incense, gold and exotic goods to the south. The voyage is shown in painted reliefs on the walls of her temple at Deir el-Bahari.

Punt's location is still debated. Most scholars place it on the African coast near today's Eritrea, Sudan and northern Ethiopia or Somalia; some include southern Arabia. Recent study of baboon mummies points to that southern Red Sea region.

The reliefs show five ships, Punt's houses on stilts, its king and his large queen, and the loading of the cargo.

  • Live myrrh trees in baskets, to plant at the temple.
  • Ebony, ivory, gold and incense resins.
  • Baboons, leopard skins and other animals.

Egypt had traded with Punt since the Old Kingdom, but Hatshepsut made this expedition a showpiece of her reign, proof of peace and wealth under a female pharaoh of the New Kingdom. It is an early example of the incense trade.
